purpose: Decide which of the user's Wiki instances, if any, should keep a local Claude Code or Codex session as raw evidence for pages written later. The user works in education (students, classes, exams, school administration) and builds agent tools in their own repositories. Most sessions are software work in those repositories whose results already live in Git, commits and specification records, so most have no lasting value. Each item is a digest of one session: a 'Project:' line with its working folder, its first user request and its last agent message; an Orca worker session is marked 'Orca worker session' and shows its task and final report. Judge only the knowledge the session leaves behind that a later page would cite, not the work it did. Choose one label.

classes.description: No lasting value; the expected label for most sessions. Belongs: work whose result is kept elsewhere, such as implementing, fixing, refactoring, reviewing, testing, committing, merging or releasing code, configuring or running tools, and writing specifications or documents that were saved to files or repositories; coordinating agents, dispatching or answering workers, status checks and progress reports; every Orca worker session whose final report describes what it changed, checked or reviewed; short answers; aborted, empty or repeated attempts. Choose another label only when the digest states a specific lesson, fact or decision with its reasons that no repository or saved file keeps and that a later page would cite.

Coding knowledge a later page would cite in any project: a specific finding about how a library, command-line tool, API, AI agent tool (for example Codex, Claude Code, Orca, mise, uv or git) or platform actually behaves, a debugging lesson with its cause, or a technical decision with its reasons, stated in the digest rather than only applied in a commit. Example: why a package manager's lock mode rejected an install and what fixed it. Does not belong: routine implementation, configuration or tool runs whose result is in a repository (none); this repository's own development history (none); education content (work). Precedence: over default for anything about software, developer tools, AI agents or programming.

Education work. Belongs: sessions about students, classes, lessons, teaching materials, exam passages and questions, grading, student records, school administration or school documents, with the facts, findings or decisions they produced, for example which exam an English reading passage came from, or how a class handout was planned. Does not belong: building or debugging software, even software for education, when the lasting value is about the code or the tool (code or none). Precedence: when a session holds both education knowledge and coding knowledge, choose work if the education knowledge is what a later page would cite. A session that names a student, guardian or school is work or none, never another wiki.

The user's web chat apps as the subject, with knowledge a later page would cite: using ChatGPT or Claude on the web, exporting or moving their conversations, browser tasks on live web pages, and offers of free AI API credit, for example how the ChatGPT data export works or which provider currently gives free credit. Does not belong: developing the chat plugin's code (code or none), education topics discussed in a chat app (work), general topics (default).

Lasting knowledge outside education, programming, developer or AI tools and web chat apps, for example a comparison made for a personal purchase, health or finance information, travel plans, or how an everyday computer or phone setting works. Rare among these sessions. Does not belong: anything about software, developer tools or AI agents (code or none), education (work), web chat apps (chat). It is not a fallback for uncertain sessions: a session without such knowledge is none.
